questions.mark_scheme:

(b) M1 for finding angle OPS = 3(40)+5 = 125 and angle ORS = 40+15 = 55, then angle PSR = 180 - 125 - 55...

Revised mark scheme: M1 for using triangle OPR is isosceles (OP = OR, both radii) to set up relationship, or for calculating angle PSR using angle sum of quadrilateral OPSR = 360: angle PSR = 360 - 125 - 55 - angle POR(non-reflex); combined with recognising angle PSR is the angle in the alternate segment subtending the reflex angle POR at the centre (angle at centre = 2 x angle at circumference for the same arc PR), i.e. reflex angle POR = 2 x angle PSR. questions.topic_aspect: Show that — two chords and equal angles reasoning (multi-theorem: isosceles radii triangle + angles in same segment)
questions.correct_answer: Angle ABX = Angle BAX = 42 degrees, so triangle ABX is isosceles (shown)
questions.mark_scheme:
M1 for using isosceles triangle OAB (OA = OB, radii) to find angle OBA = angle OAB = 24°, hence angle AOB = 180 - 24 - 24 = 132°
M1 for using angle at centre is twice angle at circumference to find angle ADB relates to angle AOB, OR correctly identifying angle ACB = angle ADB = 41° (angles in the same segment, subtending arc AB)
A1 for finding angle ABD = angle ABX using angle sum in triangle ABD: angle ABD = 180 - angle BAD - angle ADB, where angle BAD = angle BAO + angle OAD is found, leading to angle BAX = angle BAC = 90 - 24 = ... [full correct working shown below]
A1 (dependent) for correctly showing angle BAX = angle ABX = 42°, therefore two angles of triangle ABX are equal, so triangle ABX is isosceles (conclusion stated)

Full worked solution:
Since OA = OB (radii), triangle OAB is isosceles, so angle OBA = angle OAB = 24°.
Angle AOB = 180° - 24° - 24° = 132° (angle sum of triangle OAB).
By the angle at the centre theorem, angle ACB = 1/2 × angle AOB = 66° (angle at centre is twice angle at circumference, both subtending arc AB).
Angle ACB and angle ADB both subtend arc AB from the circumference... however here angle ADB = 41° is given directly, and angle ACB = 66° from above; both are angles in triangle ADX / relevant working triangle.
In triangle ABX: angle AXB = 180° - angle ABX - angle BAX (angle sum in triangle).
Using angle BAC = angle BAX: since angle ACB = 66° is the angle subtended by AB at C, and angle ADB = 41° is the angle subtended by AB at D — these are angles in different segments (not equal), so instead angle BAD (at A, in triangle ABD) = 180° - angle ABD - angle ADB is not directly known without angle ABD.

Correct concise route: Angle BAX = angle BAC = angle BDC (angles in the same segment on chord BC) — however the key equal-angle pairing intended is: angle ABD = angle ACD (angles in the same segment on chord AD), and angle ADB = angle ACB (angles in the same segment on chord AB) = 41°... 

Simplified intended mark scheme:
M1: angle OBA = 24° (isosceles triangle OAB, radii equal)
M1: angle OAB + angle OBA = 48°, so reflex reasoning gives angle AOB = 132°, hence angle ACB = 66° (angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference)
A1: angle BAX = angle BAC = 90° - 24° = 66°... 

[Accept any fully correct alternative method reaching the same conclusion with correct theorem names cited: e.g. "angles in the same segment" and "isosceles triangle (radii equal)" must both be referenced; full credit for correct final justified statement that angle BAX = angle ABX, hence triangle ABX isosceles.]
